_readme: The starter module that ships with InsightHunter: one practice, plainly described. This file is the whole content contract — swap it, or drop a content-pack.js beside the built app, to load a library of your own. See README 'Content'.

body.hips: A little higher than the knees — sit on the front edge of a cushion or chair
body.spine: Upright and stacked, following its natural curves. Tall, not braced
body.hands: Resting in the lap or on the thighs, wherever they are forgotten soonest
body.head: Balanced over the shoulders, chin very slightly down
body.gaze: Eyes closed, or open and soft on a spot a metre or two ahead
body.breath: Ordinary. You are watching it, not running it

equipment.seat: Chair, cushion, folded blanket or bench — whatever lets you sit upright without strain
equipment.surface: Stable and level; feet flat on the floor if you're on a chair
equipment.clothing: Loose enough at the waist to breathe freely
equipment.timer: Use the app's timer so you never have to check the clock

exercises.title: Sitting Meditation
exercises.keywords: sitting meditation mindfulness breath attention focus beginner basic starter
exercises.quickCue: Sit still, let the breath stay ordinary, and begin again every time you notice you have drifted. The returning is the practice.

setup: Pick a seat — chair, cushion or bench — that lets your hips sit a little above your knees
Choose somewhere you won't be interrupted for the length of the sit
Silence your phone; the timer will tell you when you're done
Decide the length before you start, and don't renegotiate it once you're sitting
movement: Sit down and let the body arrive for a few breaths before doing anything
Set the posture: upright but not stiff, hands resting, shoulders dropped
Close the eyes, or lower them to a soft point a metre or two ahead
Take three slower breaths to mark the beginning
Let the breath go back to its own rhythm — you are watching it, not steering it
Put your attention on one place where the breath is obvious: the nostrils, the chest, or the belly
Stay with one breath at a time. Not the last one, not the next one
Sooner or later you'll notice you've been thinking about something else. That noticing is the practice working
Note briefly where the mind went, without grading it, and bring attention back to the same place
Repeat that returning for the rest of the time, as many times as it takes — ten or a hundred, it makes no difference
When the bell sounds, take one deliberate breath before you move, then open your eyes slowly
mistakes: Trying to stop thinking — noticing thoughts is the practice, not a failure at it
Forcing the breath into a pattern. Let it be as boring as it wants
Sitting rigid. Upright, not braced — tension in the shoulders and jaw is the usual giveaway
Grading the sit good or bad afterwards. The only thing that counts is that you sat
Starting at forty-five minutes. Five or ten daily beats an hour once a fortnight
Checking how long is left. That's what the timer is for

variations.title: Breath Awareness
variations.cue: One place, one breath, begin again. The whole instruction fits in a sentence.
setup: Settle into the posture and take three slower breaths
Pick your spot — nostrils, chest or belly — and keep it for the whole sit
movement: Rest attention on the chosen spot
Feel the beginning, middle and end of one in-breath
Feel the small pause, then the out-breath, all the way to its end
Do that again with the next breath
When you find you've drifted, note it and come back to the same spot
Keep going until the bell
mistakes: Moving the spot around mid-sit, looking for a better one
Deepening the breath so it's easier to feel — that's a different practice
Adding effort each time you drift. Come back lightly
variations.tip: If the breath is hard to feel, rest a hand on the belly for the first minute and follow the hand instead.

variations.title: Counted Breaths
variations.cue: Count out-breaths one to ten, then start at one again. Lost count? Start at one again.
setup: Settle into the posture and take three slower breaths
Decide that the count goes on the out-breath
movement: Breathe in normally, and on the out-breath count 'one' silently
Next out-breath, 'two' — and so on up to ten
At ten, drop back to one and go again
If you notice the count has run past ten, or you can't remember the number, start again at one
Starting again is not a penalty; it's the whole exercise
Continue until the bell
mistakes: Counting so deliberately that the counting becomes louder than the breathing
Treating a lost count as evidence you're bad at this
Speeding the breath up to reach ten
variations.tip: A busy or sleepy mind holds a count better than it holds bare attention. Use this one on hard days.

variations.title: Body Settling
variations.cue: Two or three minutes of feeling where the body meets the seat, to arrive before you start.
setup: Sit down without arranging yourself yet
Let the breath do whatever it is already doing
movement: Feel the contact between your feet and the floor
Feel where your seat meets the chair or cushion, and how the weight sits on it
Feel the hands where they rest, and their temperature
Notice the whole shape of the body sitting there, all at once
Let anything that is obviously held — shoulders, jaw, forehead — go slack
Take one longer out-breath, and go on into the sit
mistakes: Turning it into a search for tension to fix
Spending the whole session here — two or three minutes is the point
variations.tip: Use this as the first step of a longer session rather than a practice on its own.

glossary.def: The one thing you keep coming back to — usually the feeling of the breath at a chosen spot. Having a single anchor is what makes it possible to notice you've left it.
What you are aware of right now. It moves on its own constantly; meditation is not about pinning it down but about noticing where it has gone and returning it.
Returning attention to the anchor after it has wandered. The single most repeated action in the practice, and the one that actually trains anything.
Watching the breath without changing it. The distinction matters: as soon as you are lengthening or deepening, you are doing a breathing exercise instead.
The places where the body meets the floor, seat or itself. Easy sensations to find, which makes them a reliable way to settle before a sit.
Attention leaving the anchor for a thought, plan or memory, usually without you noticing at the time. Expected, frequent, and not a mistake.
Naming what pulled attention away — 'planning', 'sound', 'itch' — briefly and without comment, before returning. Keeps you from getting drawn into the content.
Upright and stable enough to stay awake, relaxed enough to stay still. Chair, cushion or bench are equally valid; hips slightly above the knees is the usual advice.
One continuous sit of a decided length. Deciding the length before you start, and not renegotiating it once you're sitting, is most of the discipline.
The first minutes of a sit, where the body arrives and the obvious tension drops. Skipping it usually means spending the whole session fidgeting.
Eyes open but unfocused, resting on a spot a metre or two ahead and slightly down. An alternative to closed eyes if you get drowsy.
Not moving for the length of the sit, including small adjustments. Stillness is a decision, not a feeling — the urge to shift usually passes if you watch it instead of obeying it.
